title: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
hookLine: a morning offering, a decade, the Angelus, an evening look back

lines: FAR TOO MUCH FOR ONE DAY.
cards: Holy water at the door. Knees and bows. The Glory Be, the Creed, the morning offering, the Angelus.
The Mass scene by scene, from the Confiteor to the Sanctus to the sending. The rosary, a decade at a time. Seven sacraments.
Confession up close, the tabernacle and its red lamp, the monstrance, the holy hour. Advent, ashes, stations, the Triduum and the Exsultet.
That's what this camp has handed you since the church door: a first Mass, or a first in years. Nobody does all of that every day. So what do people actually do?

teach.b: They keep a rule of life. Rule sounds strict, but in Latin, regula first meant a straight stick, a ruler, the kind you use to draw a line or measure a wall. A rule of life is a measuring stick for your days, not a cage.
One that has lasted was written by Saint Benedict for his monks, and Benedictine monasteries still live by it: hours for prayer, for work, for reading, for meals and for sleep.
Near the end, Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners. The man tradition calls the father of Western monks thought he'd written a starter kit. You don't have to be a monk.

Plenty of lay Catholics keep a rule, some formally as Benedictine oblates or lay Franciscans or members of other third orders, and many simply on a card in their wallet. The classic small rule looks a lot like this camp.
Morning: an offering of the day before the phone. Midday: the Angelus when the noon bell rings, or a single Hail Mary. Somewhere in the day, one decade of the rosary, on a walk or in the car.
Night: a slow look back at the day, honest, not harsh. Sunday Mass. Confession now and then.
A rule isn't meant to be heroic.

teach.h: SMALL ENOUGH FOR A BAD TUESDAY.
teach.b: It's meant to be small enough to keep on a bad Tuesday, and yours enough that you'll want to. Tomorrow a new camp opens: the text itself, starting with the prayer book Benedict's monks prayed seven times a day.

how: Many Catholics keep a simple personal rule of life, such as a morning offering, the Angelus at noon, a decade of the rosary and an evening examination of conscience; some make it formal as oblates of a monastery or members of a lay third order.

o: a small, steady pattern for each day
a strict list of duties set by a priest
a vow that binds only monks and nuns

games.q: you've just finished sixty days of practices and you want to keep going. what's the classic advice?
o: do all of them, every day.
choose a few small ones and keep them daily.
wait until you feel like praying.
games.why: a rule of life is small and steady: a morning offering, the Angelus, a decade, a look back at night. even Benedict called his rule one for beginners.

practice: From everything this camp offered, choose just three things and write them down: one for the morning, one for the middle of the day, one for night.

Make each so small it's almost embarrassing: a sign of the cross, one Hail Mary, one minute looking back. If you pray, offer the three to God; if you don't, choose three small practices of attention instead.

wordCard.voice: Regula. Latin for a straight stick, a ruler, a small, steady pattern of prayer for each day, a measuring stick, not a cage. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a straight stick or ruler, then a rule. the root of our words rule and regular.

carryVoice: Your line: small, daily, mine. Day one hundred fifty-six, and with it, camp three is done.
